system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 5 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2167-11-09 13:36:00 to 2167-11-13 17:45:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a 58-year-old male with a history of acute myeloid leukemia s/p allogeneic cord blood transplant and chronic graft-versus-host disease, was admitted for acute on chronic renal failure and hyperkalemia. He experienced a brief syncopal episode upon arrival, prompting a code blue due to severe hyperkalemia, which was treated with insulin, dextrose, and kayexalate. His potassium normalized, and renal function returned to baseline. The syncopal episodes, both recent and historical, were evaluated with neurology input, leading to outpatient EEG, Holter monitor, carotid ultrasound, and echocardiogram referrals. Lisinopril was held due to hyperkalemia, Cellcept was dose-reduced, and Protonix was started for refractory gastritis. He remained stable without further events and was discharged home in good condition with follow-up arranged.
problems: Acute myeloid leukemia, without mention of having achieved remission
Other specified gastritis, without mention of hemorrhage

HISTORY:  ___ male status post bone marrow transplant, now with fever
to 101.  Please evaluate for pneumonia.

STUDY:  Upright AP portable chest radiograph.

COMPARISON:  ___.

FINDINGS:  The heart and mediastinal contours are normal.  The hila appear
normal bilaterally.  In the left lower lung, there are some band-like areas of
opacity that may represent airspace disease.  There is no hilar or mediastinal
lymphadenopathy.  There is no pleural effusion or pneumothorax.

IMPRESSION:  Left lower lobe opacities consistent with airspace space disease
and concerning for pneumonia.  These findings were communicated to ___
___ at 15:25 on ___.

CT HEAD WITHOUT CONTRAST.

COMPARISON:  ___.

HISTORY:  Altered mental status without loss of consciousness.

TECHNIQUE:  MDCT axially acquired images of the brain were obtained.  No IV
contrast was administered.

FINDINGS:  There is no evidence of acute hemorrhage or shift of normally
midline structures.  There is normal gray-white matter differentiation.  The
ventricles and sulci are normal in appearance.  There is no acute major
vascular territorial infarction.  There is no evidence of acute fracture.
There is extensive bilateral maxillary sinus mucosal thickening, left greater
than right and sphenoid sinus opacification, worse when compared to prior
exam.  The frontal sinuses are aerated.  Minimal opacification of the left
ethmoid air cells is also noted.

IMPRESSION:

1.  No evidence of acute hemorrhage.

2.  Extensive sinus disease which is slightly worse when compared to prior
exam.

MRI AND MRA OF THE HEAD.

CLINICAL INDICATION:  ___ man with history of AML, status post head
SCT and GVHD with periodic aphasic symptoms, rule out intracranial mass
lesion and stroke.

COMPARISON:  Prior CT of the head performed ___ and prior MRI
of the head dated ___.

TECHNIQUE:  MRI of the head.  Sagittal T1, sagittal T2, axial FLAIR, axial
magnetic susceptibility and diffusion-weighted sequences were performed.

MRA OF THE HEAD:

3D time-of-flight arteriography of the head was performed, multiple axial
source images as well as maximum projection images were provided.

MRA OF THE NECK:  2D time-of-flight arteriography of the vessels of the neck
were obtained, multiple rotational and axial source images were submitted for
interpretation.

FINDINGS:  There is no evidence of acute intracranial hemorrhage, mass, mass
effect, or territorial infarction.  Mild prominence of the sulci and
ventricles is identified, apparently unchanged since the most recent
examination.  Normal flow void signal is noted in the major arterial vascular
structures.  No diffusion abnormalities are detected.  On T2 and FLAIR, there
is no evidence of focal lesions.  At the convexity, the soft tissues
demonstrate a persistent and unchanged nodular formation, possibly consistent
with a sebaceous cyst.  The orbits are unremarkable, the paranasal sinuses
demonstrate slightly larger bilateral mucosal thickening involving the
maxillary sinuses and ethmoidal air cells, the mastoid air cells are grossly
normal.

IMPRESSION:  There is no evidence of acute intracranial pathology, no
diffusion abnormalities are detected.  Unchanged nodular formation at the soft
tissues at the convexity, likely related with a sebaceous cyst.

MRA OF THE HEAD:

There is evidence of vascular flow in both internal carotids as well as the
vertebrobasilar artery, there is no evidence of flow stenotic lesions or
aneurysms.

IMPRESSION:  Normal MRA of the circle of ___.

MRA OF THE NECK.

There is evidence of vascular flow in both common carotids as well as the
vertebral arteries, apparently the origin of the vessels is normal at the
vertebral arteries, the origin of the common carotids is not clearly
identified, however, apparently there is no evidence of flow stenotic lesions.

IMPRESSION:  Normal MRA of the neck.

TYPE OF EXAMINATION:  Chest PA and lateral.

INDICATION:  AML, status post endograft transplant, chronic GVHD, admitted for
febrile episode.  Assess chest concerning opacity seen on ___
AP single view chest examination.

FINDINGS:  PA and lateral chest views were obtained with patient in upright
position.  Comparison with the next preceding single AP view of ___, no significant interval change can be identified.  Thus, there exists
some linear and perivascular densities on the left base, which were not
present, at least to the same extent, on the next preceding PA and lateral
chest examination of ___.  Apparently related to clinical
manifestations, a chest CT was recommended and performed on ___.
Review of this examination demonstrates that examination demonstrated multiple
peribronchovascular ground-glass densities, nodular opacities scattered
apparently most prominent on the left lung base.  Thus, the present finding on
plain chest examination is not surprising.  It does not suggest the
development of a large discrete pneumonic infiltrate.  Considering the
history, a repeat chest CT is likely to give more detailed information
concerning progression or regression of this pulmonary process in this immune-
compromised patient.

IMPRESSION:  Stable short-term interval findings with linear and patchy
infiltrates, mostly on left lung base.  Consider CT comparison with next
preceding chest CT examination of ___.

Linear atelectasis or bronchial wall thickening and impaction at the left base

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, I'm Dr. Patel. I understand you had some episodes that felt like 'fits'—can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I was at home and suddenly I couldn’t speak right. My words were jumbled. It lasted maybe two minutes, then I was okay. Happened twice this week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Did you lose consciousness? Any shaking or weakness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I was awake. Just couldn’t talk. Felt scared, but no shaking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your history—AML, transplant, graft-versus-host disease—we need to rule out stroke or seizure. We’ll get a CT of your head right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it a stroke? I’ve been stable since the last admission.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t know yet. The CT will help. You also have a fever—101. We’re concerned about infection, so we’re starting antibiotics and doing a chest X-ray.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Fever’s been on and off. Thought it was just GVHD flaring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, but we can’t rule out pneumonia. Your chest X-ray shows some opacity in the left lower lung. We’ll monitor closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—the head CT shows no bleeding or stroke. Sinus infection is worse, but that’s not causing your speech issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s causing the 'fits' then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not sure. Could be a seizure or a neurological side effect of your medications. We’re ordering an MRI and MRA of the brain tonight to look deeper.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Seizure? I’ve never had one before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible, especially with your medical history. We’ll also check your electrolytes and B12—deficiencies can affect the brain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your respiratory viral panel came back negative. No flu or RSV. That’s good—we can focus on other causes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So not a cold?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. Your fever and lung findings may be from inflammation related to GVHD or infection we can’t see yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The MRI and MRA are back. No stroke, no tumor, no aneurysm. Your brain vessels are normal. The speech episodes aren’t from structural damage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what is it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think it could be transient neurological episodes related to your transplant or medications. We’re also checking for B-complex deficiencies—low B12 can cause this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I take supplements. Could it still be low?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, especially with GVHD affecting your gut. We’ll start B12 injections just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We repeated the chest X-ray. The lung changes are stable—no new pneumonia. The opacities are likely from chronic inflammation, not infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can stop antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll taper them. Your fever’s gone, so likely not bacterial. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs show low B12. That could be contributing to the speech episodes. We’ll continue the injections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that stop the episodes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’re also considering that your steroids for GVHD might be affecting your mood and brain function. We’re calling psychiatry to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Psychiatry? I’m not depressed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not just depression. Steroids can cause emotional disturbances—irritability, anxiety, even transient psychosis. We want to make sure we’re covering all bases.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The psychiatrist evaluated you. They think your 'fits' may be a mix of neurological and emotional factors—what we call a predominant disturbance of emotions, possibly triggered by stress and meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a seizure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can’t rule it out completely, but no EEG showed seizure activity. More likely, it’s a functional neurological episode—real symptoms, but not from structural brain damage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it happen again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, but we’re adjusting your steroids and adding B12. We’ll also refer you for outpatient therapy to help manage stress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your heart ultrasound showed mild cardiomyopathy. It’s not new, but we’ll monitor it. Also, your diabetes and cholesterol are elevated—we’ll adjust meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Diabetes? I didn’t know I had that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s secondary—likely from the steroids. We’ll start metformin and monitor your levels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been stable—no more episodes, fever gone, lungs clear. We’re planning discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What about the reflux? I’ve been having heartburn.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re adding omeprazole for esophageal reflux. Steroids can worsen that too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final chest X-ray shows improvement in the left base. No pneumonia. You’re ready for discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re discharging you today. Continue B12 injections, metformin, omeprazole, and your other meds. Follow up with hematology, neurology, and psychiatry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I have another episode?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your doctor. If it lasts more than 5 minutes or you feel weak, go to the ER. But we think the B12 and reduced steroid dose will help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad it wasn’t a stroke.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we’ve addressed several issues—B12, mood, heart, diabetes. Keep up with follow-ups, and you should do well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nursing will go over your discharge instructions. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’m good. Thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, Mr. Johnson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, one more thing—should I avoid stress?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, as much as possible. Stress can trigger these episodes. Therapy can help you build coping strategies.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make the appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good plan. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—you have all your prescriptions and follow-up details?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, got them. Hematology next week, then neurology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re all set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. Johnson. We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Discharge paperwork is signed. You’re free to go when ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate all the help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Stay well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—my wife wants to know if the 'fits' mean I can’t drive.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. Given the episodes involved speech, not consciousness, you may be able to drive, but check with neurology first. They’ll assess safety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll ask them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, better safe. Otherwise, you’re cleared.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, Doctor. Really appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. Johnson. We’re here if anything comes up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re officially discharged. Have a safe trip home.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a 58-year-old male with a history of acute myeloid leukemia s/p transplant and chronic graft-versus-host disease, was admitted after experiencing transient aphasic episodes described as 'fits.' Workup included CT and MRI of the head, which ruled out stroke, hemorrhage, or mass. Respiratory testing was negative for viral infection, and chest imaging showed stable inflammatory changes without pneumonia. He was found to have B12 deficiency, contributing to neurological symptoms, and was started on supplementation. His episodes were determined to be a mix of neurological and emotional factors, leading to a diagnosis of predominant disturbance of emotions, possibly exacerbated by steroid use. He also had secondary diabetes, hypercholesterolemia, cardiomyopathy, and esophageal reflux, all managed during admission. He improved clinically, remained stable, and was discharged with follow-up arranged in hematology, neurology, and psychiatry.
